CoMoFlow constructs protein-specific collective modes from the equilibrium structure, learns the distribution of their coefficients across the molecular dynamics (MD) ensemble, and uses sampled collective variations to guide SE(3) flow matching through feature conditioning and prior recentering. Experiments on ATLAS and de novo proteins show that CoMoFlow improves reconstruction of MD conformational distributions and coordinated structural variation relative to strong flow-based baselines, while enabling direct control over targeted conformational changes.

[530] arXiv:2611.09550 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Deliberate Pacing for Human Oversight in Agentic Software Development
Tobias Reichel, Michèle Stassen, Anamaria Mojica-Hanke, Maria Teresa Baldassarre, Sebastian Baltes, Alexander Serebrenik, Steffen Herbold
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE)

Agentic AI increasingly enables software development activities to proceed without continuous human involvement. While this autonomy may accelerate development, it also raises questions about when developers can meaningfully oversee software development done by agents. We propose deliberate pacing: intentionally adjusting when and how autonomous development proceeds to preserve opportunities for meaningful oversight. Drawing on an exploratory multivocal literature review of 20 sources, we identify three factors motivating this vision: changing relative costs of human involvement, the timing of oversight opportunities, and interdependencies between pacing decisions across the software development life cycle. We argue that neither uninterrupted autonomy nor frequent human intervention is universal. Instead, pacing should balance opportunities to understand and influence consequential decisions against costs in human attention, development time, and rework. We outline a research agenda to investigate when deliberate pacing is beneficial, how intervention timing affects oversight, and how pacing decisions interact across development activities.

[531] arXiv:2611.09552 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Towards Sustainable Federated Learning via Carbon-Aware Client Selection
Wentao Gao, Omid Tavallaie, Albert Y. Zomaya
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

The Information/Communication Technology (ICT) industry is severely challenging the global environment due to the sharply rising carbon emissions generated by machine learning (ML) workloads. Federated Learning (FL) is one of the prominent distributed ML systems used in applications with billions of client devices, such as Google Gboard and Apple Siri. Nearly half of the total carbon footprint in FL originates from client-side computation during local training. However, existing client selection strategies in FL primarily focus on minimizing energy consumption rather than carbon emissions, despite the fact that carbon impact depends not only on computational load but also on the underlying carbon intensity of the energy source. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a carbon-aware fair client selection strategy (CA-FCS) designed to minimize the carbon emissions associated with model training on client devices. In contrast to existing approaches for reducing carbon emissions in FL, we incorporate hourly carbon intensity and a realistic energy consumption model developed using empirical measurements from Google Pixel smartphones to estimate client-side carbon emissions in FL. Since repeatedly selecting low-carbon clients may reduce data diversity and degrade global model performance, particularly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data settings, CA-FCS incorporates fairness into client selection to mitigate this issue. We conduct extensive experiments under realistic FL settings for mobile devices, where client participation is constrained by device availability conditions, such as charging status and Wi-Fi connectivity. The results demonstrate that our method reduces client-side carbon emissions by up to 46% while maintaining competitive model accuracy.

[532] arXiv:2611.09554 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
Peiyu Zhang, Heng Ping, Shinibali Bhattacharyya, Anwesan Pal, Nikos Kanakaris, Kevin Cheang, Shixuan Li, Wei Yang, Paul Bogdan
Comments: 13 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at this https URL.

[533] arXiv:2611.09558 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Optimal Regret for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade
Matteo Castiglioni, Anna Lunghi, Alberto Marchesi
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Learning to profit from trade requires learning both sides of a market: what a seller is willing to accept and what a buyer is willing to pay. We study repeated bilateral trade, where an intermediary posts a purchase price to a seller and a sale price to a buyer whose valuations are drawn from an unknown joint distribution. Trade occurs only if both parties accept their respective prices, in which case the intermediary earns the difference between the two prices. The intermediary observes only whether trade occurs, without observing either valuation. We show that learning both sides of the market is no harder, in terms of regret, than learning just one. Specifically, we design an algorithm achieving regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed pair of prices, matching, up to logarithmic factors, the classical lower bound for one-dimensional dynamic pricing. Our result shows that the classical one-dimensional regret rate survives the transition to two dimensions, raising the question of whether this absence of a curse of dimensionality extends to arbitrarily high dimensions.

[534] arXiv:2611.09560 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Solver-Free Decision-Focused Learning via Neural Optimization Layers for Edge Selection
Xinda Zheng, Frits de Nijs, Edward Lam
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Decision-focused learning trains prediction models to improve downstream decisions, but many methods require costly solver calls or optimal-solution labels. We propose a solver-free decision-focused learning framework for NP-hard edge-selection problems with uncertain parameters in the objective, the constraints, or both. A neural optimization layer is first trained without solution labels, using problem objectives and constraint penalties. Graph-informed edge scoring and iterative refinement encourage concentrated and structurally consistent continuous decisions. The layer is then frozen, and a prediction model is trained through its continuous output using a problem-specific loss evaluated under observed parameters. At deployment, the predictor, optimization layer, and a lightweight decoder produce decisions without solving the original NP-hard problem. Experiments on the asymmetric traveling salesperson and endpoint-free orienteering problems show consistently better decision quality than prediction-focused learning and improvements over most evaluated decision-focused baselines. Our framework requires less training time than the evaluated decision-focused baselines, even when optimization-layer pretraining is included. Neural deployment also produces decisions faster than solver-based deployment, offering a better quality-efficiency trade-off. The layer also reduces training cost in existing decision-focused methods when used as an approximate optimization oracle.

[535] arXiv:2611.09561 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Lightweight Path-Aware Frontier Re-ranking for LiDAR-Based UAV Exploration
Duc Manh Do, Thanh Nguyen Canh, Ngoc Minh Do, Mai Thanh Thai, Xiem HoangVan
Comments: Accepted for presentation at RIVF 2026 (20th International Conference on Computing and Communication Technologies)
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Autonomous 3D exploration with UAVs requires efficient target selection under limited flight time and onboard computation. In conventional Euclidean-distance-based frontier pipelines, geometric distance may poorly represent the actual collision-free travel cost in cluttered environments, leading to inefficient frontier choices. This paper presents a lightweight path-aware frontier re-ranking method for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. The method first retains a small top-N set of promising frontier candidates using a lightweight utility function and then applies time-bounded RRT* planning to estimate their feasible path costs for re-ranking. The path generated for the selected frontier is further reused for navigation to reduce redundant global planning. Experiments in three warehouse-like environments show that the proposed method consistently produces shorter exploration trajectories than conventional frontier baselines, with traveled-distance reductions of up to 14.1%, while reducing exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments and remaining competitive in the third. The method maintains map detail comparable to the conventional OctoMap-based baseline, demonstrating an effective trade-off between exploration efficiency and mapping quality.

[536] arXiv:2611.09568 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Alignment by Confident Debate: Preference Learning from Multi-Agent Debate
Nikhil Verma, Dingxian Wang, Mohammad Reza Rezaei, Andrew Rabinovich, Zhao Chen
Comments: 53 pages, 9 Figures, 31 Tables
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Post-training language models for reasoning typically rely on gold answers, task-specific verifiers, or learned reward models, limiting scalability when such signals are scarce. Multi-agent debate offers a self-supervised alternative, but converting debate into reliable training supervision remains challenging: majority voting weights agreeing responses equally, lacks a principled tie-breaking rule, and is ill-defined for open-ended tasks without a canonical answer; likelihood-based scoring can conflate fluency with correctness; and homogeneous committees may reinforce correlated errors. We introduce Alignment by Confident Debate (AbCD), which converts debate traces into preference data without gold answer labels. A sampling-diverse committee debates each problem, after which final answers are clustered by task-level semantic equivalence. We use verifiable tasks (mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice quantitative QA, and executable code-generation) as a controlled test bed: their answer keys or executable checkers let us evaluate the quality of debate-derived supervision against ground truth, even though the oracle itself never uses gold labels. Post-training on the resulting preferences outperforms inference-only ensembling and debate, as well as SFT on the same traces, across five model families spanning 1B to 8B parameters and four datasets, improving consensus accuracy, with a maximum gain of $21.5_{pp}$. Ablations show that the approach transfers to a larger model and to code generation, while also revealing limitations of heterogeneous committees and agreement-based weighting. Overall, the results suggest that debate traces can yield useful preference supervision when answer equivalence is combined with confidence-weighted disagreement.

[537] arXiv:2611.09569 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Performance Bottlenecks in Computing ZK Proofs on a GPU
Victor Carolino, Caleb Geren, Michael Kaufman, Maximilian Nussbaum, William Scott, Henry F. Korth
Comments: 8 pages
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Zero-knowledge proofs allow one party to prove the correctness of a statement or execution of a computation while revealing no more than the statement of correctness itself. Recent use cases, such as AI datasets, suggest the need for faster proof generation over increasingly large constraint sets. This paper explores efforts in optimizing zero-knowledge proof generation, specifically PlonK, using GPUs, for applications that are not amenable to solution via incrementally verifiable computing (IVC).
Our intention with this work is to improve ZK performance by introducing fundamental changes in the low-level architectural structure of proof generation. These changes affect performance curves for most current proof
generation algorithms. In particular, this paper explores the trade-offs between increased parallelization on GPUs and the resultant memory management problems that occur due to this parallelization. We implement a parallelized PlonK in order to analyze these trade-offs and make arguments concerning the nature of data flows within the proving protocol. Our results lead us to consider multi-GPU environments to maximize performance for large circuit sizes. Such environments introduce issues of communication, efficient hardware management, data partition, and data
transfers. This paper further discusses the use cases that motivate multi-GPU implementations, their cost models, and the use of remote direct memory access (RDMA) for data transfer among GPUs.

[538] arXiv:2611.09570 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Video Stitching from Multiple Moving Cameras
Shira Ifergane, Roy Amoyal, Shahar Benishay, Oren Freifeld
Comments: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

We address geometric video alignment for the same scene captured by multiple freely moving cameras. Existing methods, which are based on image stitching or video stabilization, are typically limited to two cameras or must assume the restrictive setting of a fixed linear ordering of the cameras. We propose MViS, a lightweight test-time optimization framework for joint multi-view alignment with temporal consistency. MViS uses a spatial-transformer-inspired net to jointly process frames from all views within a short temporal window and predict per-view, per-time homographies. Optimization proceeds in two stages: geometry-guided alignment followed by appearance-based refinement, with both stages enforcing multi-view and temporal consistency across the sequence. The method requires no scene-specific hyperparameter tuning, handles arbitrary and time-varying view-intersection graphs, and remains robust under rapid camera motion. On a standard two-view video benchmark, MViS matches or surpasses the state of the art. To facilitate evaluation in more complex scenarios, we introduce an annotated dataset with more than two freely moving cameras and establish the first benchmark for this setting. Project page: this https URL .

[539] arXiv:2611.09571 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Symmetric Zassenhaus splittings for bounded and unbounded operators
Paul Bergold, Arieh Iserles, Karolina Kropielnicka
Comments: First version. 34 pages
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

We establish rigorous local-error bounds for the entire family of symmetric Zassenhaus splittings for possibly unbounded operators, under explicit assumptions on commutator bounds, regularity-preserving flows, and conjugation identities. Truncated symmetric Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansions yield an explicit coefficient formula for the Zassenhaus exponents and identify vanishing commutator expressions. In order to extend these cancellations to the realm of unbounded operators, we prove a general theorem on finite expansions of multiple operator conjugations with controlled integral remainders. For splittings of order 2n, our argument gives the sufficient commutator-length bound 4n-1, revealing regularity requirements that are not apparent from the formal order calculation. Using the Schrödinger equation with a quadratic potential as an example, we show that the order-dependent regularity requirements can reduce to one fixed weighted Sobolev space for all splitting orders.

[540] arXiv:2611.09574 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Bayesian Inverse Problems for EUV reflectometry with regularized JKO scheme
Vitalii Aksenov, Oliver Henze
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

We study a Bayesian inverse problem in EUV reflectometry, where optical constants and layer thicknesses are inferred from angle- and wavelength-resolved reflection measurements. The physical process is modeled and evaluated using an efficient forward model based on the transfer matrix method. As an alternative to computationally expensive sampling-based inference, we employ an Eulerian, entropically regularized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme that minimizes the Kullback--Leibler divergence via proximal steps in the Wasserstein space. Using the Benamou--Brenier dynamic formulation and a Hopf-Cole transform, each JKO step is reformulated as a pair of heat equations coupled only through their initial and terminal conditions, enabling an efficient fixed-point solver. The resulting high-dimensional densities are discretized on tensor-product grids and represented in tensor-train format, exploiting Kronecker structure for scalable computation. Preconditioning based on estimated posterior moments further improves tractability. We test the method with numerical experiments on EUV reflectometry data for a ruthenium--silicon ($\ce{Ru}$ on $\ce{Si}$) specimen and compare the learned tensor-train posterior to ensemble Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) reference samples. We demonstrate a use case in which we are able to reuse the tensor-train posterior to obtain samples for shifted target distributions with less computational effort than a comparable MCMC method.

[541] arXiv:2611.09575 [pdf, html, other]
Title: An Empirical Evaluation of a Weighted PALU Model for Internet Traffic Networks
Wood Moore, Hayden Jananthan, Jeremy Kepner
Comments: 5 pages, 1 figure, IEEE MIT URTC 2026
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)

The PALU model is a hybrid power law generative framework that decomposes Internet traffic graphs into three structural components: a preferential attachment core, degree one leaf nodes, and disconnected satellite clusters. Although the original PALU formulation provided a theoretical basis for this decomposition, it was never validated against real traffic data and was restricted to unweighted networks. This work presents the first empirical evaluation of PALU against real Internet traffic, using packet traces from the MAWI WIDE samplepoint F dataset. We introduce a weighted extension of the model incorporating strength degree scaling, and develop a packet-to-graph pipeline for parameter estimation across multiple observation window sizes. Results show that the power law degree exponent $\alpha \approx 2.0$ remains stable across observation scales from $10^5$ to $3 \times 10^6$ packets, consistent with the PALU structural prediction. However, the satellite cluster parameter $\lambda$ and the weighted scaling parameter $\theta$ exhibit systematic dependence on observation scale, and the Poisson star assumption for unattached components is formally rejected at all tested window sizes. These results indicate that PALU captures important aspects of Internet traffic structure but requires an explicit observation model to fully account for finite sampling effects.

[542] arXiv:2611.09583 [pdf, html, other]
Title: MSR-ABC: Complementary Feature Fusion for Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
Comments: Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) classification from computed tomography (CT) may benefit from representations that capture different aspects of tumour phenotype. However, simply concatenating reconstruction-derived features, image--text embeddings, and radiomic descriptors may not fully exploit their complementary information. We propose MSR-ABC, a global--local framework integrating MedVAE, MedSigLIP, and radiomics. Spatially matched local image descriptors interact through cross-representation attention, while radiomic auxiliary supervision encourages the pooled local representation to retain quantitative tumour attributes. A gated residual mechanism integrates local information with global summaries. Area-aware pooling and visual and soft-text prompting complete the framework. We evaluate discrimination using a patient-level split of 396 KiTS23 cases and an external cohort of 111 TCGA/TCIA cases, reporting mean AUROC over three training seeds with 95% patient-bootstrap confidence intervals. MSR-ABC achieves mean AUROCs of 0.806 internally and 0.879 externally. Internally, it exceeds global MedVAE--radiomics and three-source concatenation by 3.35 and 3.61 AUROC percentage points, respectively. Removing any source lowers mean AUROC in both cohorts, with the largest decreases following radiomics removal. Individual removal of cross-representation attention, auxiliary supervision, or gated fusion also lowers internal mean AUROC. These findings are consistent with complementary contributions within the integrated architecture and support further investigation of structured representation fusion for non-invasive renal tumour characterisation.

[543] arXiv:2611.09584 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Extended Model-Based Learned Inertial Odometry
Sasanka Kuruppu Arachchige, Joni-Kristian Kämäräinen
Comments: 8 pages, Published at ICUAS 2026
Journal-ref: ICUAS 2026
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Inertial odometry is a compelling approach to state estimation for agile quadrotor flight due to its affordability, low weight, and robustness to perceptual degradation. However, relying only on integrated inertial measurements is impractical, as sensor errors and time-varying biases lead to significant pose drift. Although recent advances have enabled inertial odometry for drone racing, existing approaches show limited generalization to trajectories not seen during training. This work improves generalization by adopting a body-frame representation and incorporating body-frame torque dynamics into the learning pipeline. The learned model predicts short-horizon relative displacements, which are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for quadrotor pose estimation on unseen trajectories. An additional evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets, with whole trajectory shapes held out of training, confirms a lower velocity error on every held-out set and shows that the torque input is most informative when it is derived from the rotor signals. Code, data pipeline and trained models are publicly available.

[544] arXiv:2611.09585 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Scalable Full-Horizon SFC Deployment over Predictable SAGIN Topologies via Configurable Column Generation Framework
Hang Li, Hao Huang, Yihu Xu, Zixuan Kong, Yanling Jin
Comments: 18 pages, 10 figures, 4 tables
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)

Space-air-ground integrated networks (SAGINs) integrate heterogeneous communication and computing resources to support ubiquitous services. Service function chains (SFCs) enable complex services to be composed of ordered functions and executed collaboratively across these resources. Mobility continuously reshapes connectivity throughout service execution, yet much of the resulting topology evolution is predictable. Decisions based only on isolated topology snapshots may therefore overlook valuable future connectivity. We formulate an admission-first, cost-aware model on a time-expanded graph for SFC deployment. Our key observation is that temporal feasibility is request-specific, whereas global coupling arises mainly from shared-resource competition. We therefore develop a configurable column-generation framework in which complete request deployments form columns and a restricted master problem coordinates admission and resources. SAGINFE, a fast constructive heuristic built on per-flow embedding (PFE), supplies a standalone feasible solution and initial columns. Configurable pricing schedules combine early-terminated and stricter searches, supplemented by selective PFE candidates. Candidates undergo feasibility and exact reduced-cost checks. Request-wise pricing can run in parallel, followed by finite-pool integer selection. The default configuration improves the admission-first objective over initialization on all 120 main instances. Four pricing workers achieve up to a 2.69-fold median pricing-stage speedup while preserving admitted request counts in the tested cases.

[545] arXiv:2611.09589 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Dual-Number Associative Arrays for One-Pass Provenance and Sensitivity
Timothy Habashy, Hayden Jananthan, Jeremy Kepner
Comments: 5 pages, 1 figure
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

Associative arrays and GraphBLAS express sparse computations as matrix operations over a chosen semiring, but the result normally contains only the ordinary value. We define a dual-number extension $D_k(S)=S\ltimes S^k$ that carries this value together with $k$ independent auxiliary channels in the same computation. We prove that the construction is a split square-zero extension of any commutative semiring. Over min-plus, the auxiliary value is the weight of the shortest walk constrained to use the corresponding edge, excluding the weight of that edge. This gives an exact shortest-path membership test for that edge, although ties return the union of the edges on all optimal paths. We implement the min-plus construction using sparse \texttt{python-graphblas} operations, with a fixpoint test that checks the value and auxiliary components together. We validate the implementation across 18,692 checks, including 2,825 tied target pairs. On random graphs with 100,000 vertices and 32 seed edges, the dual method is $3.39\times$ faster than the sequential algorithm but $1.50\times$ slower than a min-plus-specific batched method. This difference is largely explained by the dual method requiring $1.55\times$ as many sweeps. Thus, the main contribution is a general algebraic approach with competitive sparse performance, rather than information that specialized min-plus algorithms cannot already compute.

[546] arXiv:2611.09593 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Coarse-to-Fine Finite Element Solver for Heterogeneous Darcy Flow
Kapil Chawla, Sanghyun Lee, Jonathan Valyou
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

Quantum linear system algorithms offer theoretical potential for solving large sparse systems from PDE discretizations. However, applying them directly to fine-scale problems remains impractical on near-term hardware because of limited qubits, restricted circuit depth, and noise. They also prepare a quantum state rather than solution coefficients, whose recovery requires measurement and reconstruction.
In this work, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical coarse-to-fine finite element framework for heterogeneous Darcy flow. We investigate whether a measured quantum coarse solution improves fine-grid initialization and reduces subsequent classical solver work. Rather than solve the full fine-scale system on a quantum device, we apply a method inspired by the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) to the Galerkin coarse system. We reconstruct the approximate coarse solution from measurements, prolongate it to the fine grid, and use it to initialize a classical preconditioned iterative solve.} Numerical experiments on steady heterogeneous Darcy flow and a time-dependent SPE10-based problem show that measured quantum coarse solutions can improve fine-grid initialization, while classical correction recovers accurate pressure fields. The effect on classical solver iterations depends on the problem. All quantum computations were simulated using Qiskit Aer.

[547] arXiv:2611.09596 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Coordinatewise Epsilon for Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
Jeonseong Kim, Chenglin Fan
Comments: 32 pages
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Adam estimates second moments coordinatewise, but typically adds the same scalar $\varepsilon$ to every denominator. We study how this shared $\varepsilon$ affects convergence when noise and curvature vary across coordinates. Under coordinatewise finite-$p$ noise moments, $p\in(1,2]$, choosing $\varepsilon_i$ from the noise and curvature bounds for each coordinate attains the heavy-tailed $\ell_1$-stationarity benchmark $O(T^{-\frac{p-1}{3p-2}})$, matching the known optimal time exponent for smooth nonconvex stochastic optimization. For $1<p<2$, Adam with a shared $\varepsilon_t$ admits a lower bound of order $\Omega(T^{-\frac{p-1}{2p}})$. This lower bound holds for every predictable scalar choice of $\eta_t$, $\beta_{1,t}$, $\beta_{2,t}$, and $\varepsilon_t$, precluding a dimension-uniform benchmark rate for this class.

[548] arXiv:2611.09597 [pdf, html, other]
Title: RuACT: Recovering Inactive Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers
Yijun Li, Zhengxi Lu, Zhipiao Liu, Jinzheng Yu, Xutao Weng, Jian Shao, Yongliang Shen
Comments: 22 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Rubric-based reinforcement learning (RL) extends RL with verifiable rewards to open-ended tasks by scoring each response against query-specific rubrics. Under group-relative optimization, however, a rubric that every sampled response fails (unreachable) or passes (saturated) gives all responses the same outcome and no learning signal; in Qwen3-4B medical training, 60.88% of query-rubric observations are inactive. We find that the two states lack different supervision: stating an unreachable rubric in the prompt raises its satisfaction from 1.13% to 91.25%, whereas responses that all pass a saturated rubric still differ in quality. We therefore propose RuACT (Rubrics as Adaptive Critics and Teachers), which assigns each inactive rubric the role that supplies what it lacks. Rubric as Teacher uses unreachable rubrics as privileged information for reward-gated on-policy self-distillation, and Rubric as Critic decomposes saturated rubrics into child rubrics that separate current responses while sharing the parent's weight. RuACT outperforms GRPO, rubric reweighting, and rubric-guided exploration on all four medical and scientific benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and achieves the best average with Qwen3-1.7B. On initially unreachable rubrics, unguided recovery rises from 35.02% to 42.86%, while child refinement improves reward-quality alignment on independent rollouts from 57.74% to 60.77%. Code is available at this https URL.

[549] arXiv:2611.09598 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Transformer-FSQ: Discrete Latents for Extreme KV-Cache Compression
Andras Szecsenyi, Thomas L. Lee, Vaisakh Shaj, Elliot J. Crowley, Amos Storkey
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Private, personalised language models must run on local consumer devices, where large, frontier models cannot fit, and retaining long contexts is non-trivial. Sequential memory---the key-value (KV) cache---grows linearly with context length, quickly dwarfing the model itself: for Qwen3-1.7B-Base, 200,000 retained entries require 21 GiB, 6.6 times more than the model weights. Yet the KV-cache compression methods we measured fail beyond moderate compression ratios. We introduce Transformer-FSQ, addressing extreme KV-cache compression by replacing standard key and value projections with a finite scalar quantisation bottleneck. Our cache stores a packed vector of discrete integer codes per token, with no per-token quantisation metadata. Converting a pretrained transformer trains only these projections on 0.25 tokens per original parameter. We evaluate Transformer-FSQ against five baseline families on models from 0.6B to 8B parameters. On long-context retrieval (RULER), from 12$\times$ to 97.5$\times$ Transformer-FSQ is the most accurate method we evaluate, across scales. A fused Triton kernel decodes directly from the integer codes; with baselines given their authors' kernels where available, it decodes at $1.01\times$ (95% interval $0.98$--$1.05$) the throughput of native SDPA attention on the uncompressed Qwen3-8B-Base at $32\times$ and $1.54\times$ at $97.5\times$. Extreme KV-cache compression is therefore a practical way to extend how much context a fixed device can hold.

[550] arXiv:2611.09599 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Dual-Region Slice Aggregation for CT-Based Renal Tumor Classification
Yuan Liang, Sourav Bhattacharjee, Abraham Campbell
Comments: Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common kidney cancer in adults. We present a region-aware architecture for CT-based ccRCC classification. Tumor and 0--10 mm peritumoral context are pooled separately from shared frozen DINOv3 feature maps. A shared position-aware slice aggregator precedes fixed training-only principal component analysis (PCA). The resulting representations are fused with radiomics using two scalar feature gates. Evaluation on KiTS23 and 111 external cases yields internal test and external AUCs of 0.8078\pm0.0154 and 0.9094\pm0.0015. Compared with matched single-tumor readout, mean AUC increases by 1.50 and 2.34 percentage points, respectively. Early-PCA and reconstruction controls yield lower internal mean AUCs, while external AUC is similar for early and late PCA. These findings highlight the joint role of regional readout and slice aggregation in adapting frozen visual features to renal CT.

[551] arXiv:2611.09600 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Coresets for Capacitated Clustering via Dual Concentration
Milind Prabhu, Chris Schwiegelshohn, Sudarshan Shyam, Erik Waingarten
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We study coresets for clustering problems, focusing on the classical $k$-median and $k$-means objectives. A coreset is a small weighted summary of the input data that approximately preserves the clustering cost for every choice of centers. Such summaries are a central tool for scaling clustering algorithms to large datasets.
In this work, we consider the capacitated setting, where the clustering is subject not only to choosing centers but also to respecting prescribed cluster-size constraints. This model is a natural generalization of standard clustering and has been widely studied, but its coreset complexity is less well understood. For finite metric spaces, we obtain optimal-size coresets; surprisingly, these match the best-known bounds for unconstrained clustering. We also give improved coreset bounds in Euclidean space, notably the first coresets with near-linear dependence in $k$ while being independent of the dimension and input size.
The main new technical ingredients are concentration bounds for the dual solutions of min-cost flow problems, which allow for both significantly simpler and tighter analyses of the underlying sampling distribution used in the coreset construction.

[552] arXiv:2611.09601 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Fast and Accurate Algorithm for the $p \to q$ Norm of Sparse Non-Negative Matrices
Marco Pirazzini, Daniel A. Spielman
Comments: 31 pages, 6 figures
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We present an algorithm that computes the $p \to q$ norm of a non-negative matrix with $s$ nonzero entries to accuracy $\varepsilon$ in time $\widetilde{O}(s^{3/2} \log (1/\varepsilon))$, for any $p \ge q \ge 1$. The fastest algorithm previously designed for this problem has running time $\widetilde{O}(s / \varepsilon)$ (Objois and Vladu, 2026), which is slower when high accuracy solutions are desired.
Our algorithm employs a surprising application of Laplacian solvers inside an Interior Point Method (IPM). We formulate the problem as a linear optimization problem over a product of power cones, and show that the Newton updates of the IPM can be computed by solving a Laplacian system in a Schur complement after subtracting a rank-2 matrix.
We also discuss an implementation of our algorithm, showing that it is practical and it outperforms optimized solvers such as MOSEK by factors of up to $20\times$ on a variety of tasks.

[553] arXiv:2611.09605 [pdf, html, other]
Title: DKWBC: Decoupling Motion Tracking and Balancing for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
Dingkun Wei, Zehong Shen, Huaijin Pi, Xueyang Wang, Xing Zhu, Hujun Bao, Yujun Shen, Xiaowei Zhou
Comments: 9 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Humanoid whole-body control requires a robot to track diverse reference motions while maintaining balance under gravity, torque limits, contact switching, and external disturbances. Existing reinforcement-learning-based trackers typically learn control outputs that jointly address motion tracking and balance. However, similar reference poses can correspond to substantially different dynamic demands, requiring a unified policy to learn motion-dependent control requirements alongside balance corrections. This can complicate learning and lead to high-frequency fluctuations in control outputs. We propose DKWBC, a dynamics-informed whole-body control framework that combines explicit model-based tracking with a learned balancing residual. Inspired by the model-based and environmental-wrench contributions to joint torques in floating-base dynamics, DKWBC uses inverse-dynamics feedforward and joint PD feedback to supply tracking torques, while a residual policy learns additional joint-torque corrections for balanced execution. By explicitly accounting for motion-dependent torque demands, this structure simplifies the policy's learning task. Experiments in simulation and on real hardware demonstrate that a single learned balancing policy generalizes across motion datasets while maintaining accurate motion tracking and balance across ground support, attached payloads, and physical interaction. Project page: this https URL.

[554] arXiv:2611.09607 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ReplayAudit: Auditing Outsourced LLM Fine-Tuning via Sealed Records and Selective Replay
Yihan Xia, Wenxin Xu, Taotao Wang
Comments: 23 pages, 5 figures
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.

[555] arXiv:2611.09609 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
Karina Romanova, Igor Kiselev, Vladimir Platonov, Viliana Devbunova, Gregory Leleytner, Adeliya Leleytner, Lina Veltman, Aleksandr Nikolich
Comments: 21 pages. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-Term Memory for AI Systems (PALM)
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains inconclusive. A small movie-tagging experiment with one training seed also finds no advantage over other users' histories. These findings show why personalization should be evaluated on unseen users, with histories of similar content and a model trained without history as comparisons. We also find that adding gated cross-attention improves on a prefix-only model under our training setup; whether this holds more broadly remains open.

[556] arXiv:2611.09611 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Online Timely Bin Packing Revisited: A Simpler Algorithm with Optimality in Special Cases
Pei-Lin Chiang, Wing-Kai Hon, Ying-Chia Huang, Li-Tzu Yang
Comments: 17 pages, 1 figure
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

Online Timely Bin Packing is a variant of classical online bin packing in which items arrive over time with sizes and deadlines. Packing an item may be deferred until its deadline, but once a collection of items is packed into a bin, the bin is closed and cannot be used again. The objective is to minimize the total number of bins used. The problem was introduced by Khattar in 2023. In 2025, Aminian proposed Discrete-Greedy, a deterministic online algorithm with a competitive ratio of exactly $2$, which remains the best-known upper bound. Its analysis is particularly simple; however, the algorithm requires maintaining a fractional simulation internally and may leave usable space in some bins unfilled.
We propose Thrifty-Greedy, a simple deterministic online algorithm that does not require a fractional simulation. We prove that its competitive ratio is exactly $2$, matching the best-known upper bound. At the same time, the algorithm automatically achieves the optimal competitive ratio on two natural classes of inputs: it is $1$-competitive when all items have the same size, and $1.5$-competitive when every item has size in $\{1/3,2/3\}$. In contrast, Discrete-Greedy has a competitive ratio of at least $2$ on both classes.

[557] arXiv:2611.09614 [pdf, other]
Title: Know What You Need: Efficient Activation Checkpointing
Danyal Ahmed (MLIA), Edouard Oyallon (MLIA)
Journal-ref: The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems, 2026, Paris, France
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Large Language Model training is increasingly constrained by memory capacity. Activation Checkpointing reduces activation memory by avoiding storing selected activations during the forward pass and rematerializing them during backpropagation, thereby trading memory savings for additional computation. Although this technique is essential for scaling model training, rematerialization can be prohibitively expensive, particularly for Transformer linear layers. Approximate computation could reduce this overhead, but conventional approaches either introduce errors that accumulate over the backward pass or fail to exploit information available from the initial forward pass. We introduce a novel approximate rematerialization method that can yield unbiased gradient estimates: using information collected during the initial forward pass, the method selectively recomputes only the most important layer components, either through greedy selection or randomized sketching. Ablation studies show that the resulting gradients closely match the exact gradients. When applied to feed-forward layers, attention layers, or both, our method can recompute only two-thirds of the layer components in a Llama-488M model, while increasing perplexity by just 1.7%, 1.2%, and 2.5%, respectively.

[558] arXiv:2611.09615 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
Romain Cosson, Federico Fusco, Anupam Gupta, Stefano Leonardi, Renato Paes Leme, Matteo Russo
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds.
For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt \Sigma)$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_B})$, where $\Sigma_S$ and $\Sigma_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations.
We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

[559] arXiv:2611.09616 [pdf, html, other]
Title: SparseModesNet for coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical system in heterogeneous porous media
Kapil Chawla, Tomoki Koike, Sanghyun Lee, Julie Bessac
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA); Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) models describe interactions among displacement, fluid pressure, and temperature in geothermal systems. Fine-mesh simulations over many time steps are costly, particularly with heterogeneous permeability and thermal conductivity or fracture networks that alter fluid and heat transport. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduces the number of unknowns but can require many modes because its reconstruction is linear. We apply SparseModesNet to reconstruct coupled THM solutions using a small set of selected modes and a neural-network nonlinear decoder. Starting from a larger collection of candidate modes, SparseModesNet selects modes to reduce reconstruction error rather than simply retaining those with the highest energy. We compare SparseModesNet with POD on three problems: a two-dimensional heterogeneous medium, a two-dimensional connected fracture network, and a three-dimensional geometry based on Utah FORGE fractures. We evaluate reconstructed displacement, pressure, and temperature fields, as well as pressure- and temperature-based quantities of interest. We also test temporal interpolation by training on a subset of snapshots and reconstructing omitted snapshots within the same time interval. For the same reduced dimension, SparseModesNet achieves smaller reconstruction errors than POD and accurately recovers the solution fields and selected geothermal quantities of interest.

[560] arXiv:2611.09617 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CRTrack-Cap: A New Benchmark for Cross-View Dense Video Object Captioning
Xiangqun Zhang, Likai Wang, Zekun Qian, Rui Zhou, Ruize Han, Wei Feng
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.

[561] arXiv:2611.09621 [pdf, html, other]
Title: BiLoGo: Reducing the smoothing of localised responses in Transformer-based neural operators for sheet forming
Yingxue Zhao, Haoran Li, Haosu Zhou, Tobias Pfaff, Nan Li
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Trial-and-error FE simulation of sheet forming could be computationally expensive, neural-network-based learned simulators are used to accelerate design. These simulators should accurately capture localised responses, such as thinning around sharp radii or near ribs, which determine formability. Transformer-based neural operators propagate information efficiently across the mesh but tend to smooth such localised responses. This study develops BiLoGo, a Bipartite Local-Global learned simulator with an FE-guided design that connects local node-element message passing with a Transformer-based neural operator for long-range information exchange. BiLoGo has three modules: a bidirectional node-element GraphSAGE model that learns nodal-elemental coupling on a bipartite graph and predicts each quantity on its native FE entity without interpolation; a dual-stream Transformer-based neural operator that processes blank deformation and tool contact with separate token sets, preventing localised contact information from being averaged with the whole-blank state; and a fusion and element update module that combines global and local features via gated residual fusion and updates element features conditioned on element-node kinematics. Evaluated on a dome-shaped cold forming case and two corner-shaped hot stamping cases (one with ribs), BiLoGo achieves the lowest positional and threshold-based thinning errors on all three cases compared with single-level and hierarchical graph-based models and Transformer-based neural operators. Near the ribs, the smoothing index of predicted thinning increases from 0.41-0.56 for Transformer-based neural operators to 0.94 for BiLoGo-U. Compared with the hierarchical graph network CAtt-BiUGNN, BiLoGo-T reduces mean positional error by 15.5% on the Corner case and BiLoGo-U by 8.3% on the Corner+Rib case, with 66-69% less training memory.

[562] arXiv:2611.09622 [pdf, html, other]
Title: On Positive Computation
Eduardo Skapinakis
Subjects: Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)

We introduce new notions of reducibility for monotone classes and show that a monotone version of Circuit Satisfiability and the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem are complete for $mNP$, even under positive reductions (which are not the same as monotone reductions). If this holds for all (monotone) $mNP$-complete problems - that they are also so complete for $mNP$ -, then $P\neq NP$. We introduce positive models of relativized computation and show that the separation $posP\subsetneq mNP$ does not relativize, even when oracles are restricted to monotone sets. Yet, there is a (weak) diagonalization proof that $posP\subsetneq mNP$.

[563] arXiv:2611.09623 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Entering a New Domain in the Era of Generative AI: An Autoethnography of Solo Game Development as a Bioinformatics Educator
Hannah Kim
Comments: 12 pages, 1 figure
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

The rapid improvement of generative AI (GenAI) not only increased the efficiency of practice but also empowered individuals with capabilities to explore new domains. However, identity formation in the wake of such empowerment remains understudied. We use an autoethnography to understand identity formation in the context of solo game development as a bioinformatics educator. With the goal of developing a create-your-own-adventure (CYOA) game, we collected data for 73 days through journal entries, interacting with communities of practices. The autoethnographer had continuously reassessed the situation, and closely interacted with communities of practice. Their prior knowledge was used to provide in-game context and to uniquely interpret game development processes. These findings suggest that the autoethnographer made efforts to belong to communities of practice and engaged extensively in sensemaking through the lens of a bioinformatics educator. Although GenAI puts power at hand, attaining a new identity took place at a human pace.

[564] arXiv:2611.09624 [pdf, html, other]
Title: TPIC: Energy-Conserving Space Plasma Simulations on GPU Supercomputers
Luca Pennati, Ivy Peng, Stefano Markidis
Subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF)

Artificial heating and numerical damping affect particle energization in kinetic space plasma simulations, even when the numerical scheme remains stable. Implicit and semi implicit energy conserving Particle-in-Cell (PIC) methods eliminate these errors in the discrete energy balance while relaxing explicit stability constraints. We present TPIC, a massively parallel implementation of the Energy Conserving Semi-Implicit Method (ECSIM) for GPU supercomputers. We extend the exact energy conservation in the ECSIM formulation to closed domains with conducting boundaries by deriving and canceling a spurious term in the discrete Poynting flux theorem. TPIC executes the complete particle and field cycle on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, combining matrix-engine acceleration with asynchronous communication and computation. We validate TPIC in a variety of electrostatic and electrodynamic test cases relevant for space plasma physics applications, including quasineutral plasma expansion, two-stream instability, Whistler waves, Weibel instability, Whistler turbulence, and three-dimensional magnetic reconnection with conducting walls and 12.3 billion particles. We show that in all scenarios, TPIC agrees with the corresponding analytical theory or reference numerical results, and preserves the total system energy to machine precision. On 4,096 AMD GPUs, TPIC advances 1.9 trillion particles with 96.8\% weak scaling efficiency.

[565] arXiv:2611.09625 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
Maxime Burchi, Fayaz Ali Dharejo, Radu Timofte
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k.

[566] arXiv:2611.09626 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Novel Algorithm to Simulate Conductance-based Neuronal Networks
Amir Shahhosseini, Rodolphe Sepulchre
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Conductance-based models are central to neurophysiology and neuromorphic engineering, yet their simulation scales poorly to large networks. We study and analyze an iterative solver that operates in signal space. Each iteration reduces to $N$ decoupled scalar linear time-varying differential equations, one per neuron, which are solved in parallel and in closed form. The solver admits two complementary interpretations: a variable metric forward-backward splitting method, rooted in operator theory, and a waveform relaxation quasi-Newton method, rooted in circuit simulation. We prove uniform and superlinear convergence, with a bound that reflects the conductance structure of the dynamics. The algorithm is illustrated on the classical Hodgkin--Huxley neuron and on networks of up to 5000 neurons.

[567] arXiv:2611.09627 [pdf, html, other]
Title: What remains of the planar induced minor conjectures?
Jadwiga Czyżewska, Tomáš Masařík, Marcin Pilipczuk, Paweł Rzążewski
Comments: 26 pages, 7 figures
Subjects: Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM); Computational Complexity (cs.CC); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Combinatorics (math.CO)

Dallard, Milanič, and Štorgel, and independently Gartland and Lokshtanov, conjectured that for every planar graph $H$, Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring are polynomial-time solvable in $H$-induced-minor-free graphs. As a structural explanation, Gartland and Lokshtanov further conjectured that such graphs admit balanced separators dominated by a constant number of vertices. Bonnet and Chang recently refuted the independent-set part of the algorithmic conjecture, by showing that Maximum Independent Set is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in graphs excluding the $5\times5$ grid as an induced minor.
We revisit both conjectures. We show that the graphs used by Bonnet and Chang exclude much simpler planar graphs, including several $16$-vertex trees, and we introduce a second, independent family of hard instances. We also prove that $3$-Coloring is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard in both settings, thus refuting the algorithmic conjecture in full, even in its quasipolynomial version, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathsf{QP}$. On the structural side, we identify planar graphs $H$ for which the structural conjecture holds, while the algorithmic one fails. Thus, constantly dominated balanced separators cannot by themselves explain the tractability of Maximum Weight Independent Set and List $3$-Coloring.

[568] arXiv:2611.09634 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
Constantinos Karouzos, Nikolaos Aletras
Comments: Preprint. Under review
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

[569] arXiv:2611.09636 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Capacity of Generic Symmetric Distributed Linear Computation: The Geometry of Relations
Hua Sun
Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT)

In distributed linear computation, $K$ users observe linear functions of common finite-field data and send separate messages to a server that wants another linear function. We characterize the generic capacity $C$, the minimum total number of field symbols sent per computed instance, when all observations and the demand have dimension $\nu$, the data have dimension $\mu$, and the coefficients of these linear functions are drawn independently and uniformly from the field and stay fixed during coding, with the field size growing through arbitrary prime powers. For fixed $K$, $C/\nu$ depends only on $\tau=\mu/\nu$: the curve has finitely many linear pieces for at most three users, infinitely many pieces approaching one value of $\tau$ for four users, and a rational part between two sequences of linear pieces for five or more users. The geometry of the relation space, formed by the linear relations among the observations and the demand, determines three things: the shape of the curve, which relations the coding scheme aligns, and the entropy inequalities used in the converse. Generically, the user subspaces of this space are either balanced, where the capacity lies on a single rational curve, or split into two balanced components, a sparse and a dense one, which produces the linear pieces. Achievability uses asymptotic set alignment, in which monomial precoders confine the combined observation differences to a small set. The converse uses the same geometry to lower-bound the sum of the users' remaining observation entropies in terms of the remaining data entropy.

[570] arXiv:2611.09640 [pdf, html, other]
Title: LACART: Lookahead-Augmented Collision Avoidance and Reference Tracking Strategies for Safety-Critical Robots
Pedro Lopes, Amit Shivam, Luis Tiago Paiva
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Autonomous racing provides a demanding testbed for collision avoidance under tight geometric and computational constraints. Building on a recent conference contribution and a master's dissertation, LACART combines lookahead-based control barrier functions (CBFs), a relaxed control Lyapunov function (CLF), and quadratic programming (QP) to modify nominal vehicle commands for obstacle avoidance and reference tracking. The method handles circular obstacles and track boundaries in a common optimisation layer. Comparative simulation results against Huang \emph{et al.} \cite{r9} show similar full-track paths and lower median computation times: 0.31 versus 0.33 ms per step and 0.023 versus 0.025 ms per QP solve. The dissertation further demonstrates a 1:43-scale vehicle with camera-based estimation and wireless actuation at a reported 25 Hz control rate. We identify the conditions linking lookahead-point clearance to body clearance, illustrate hardware limitations, and propose a recorded demonstration of safety intervention and recovery. The contribution targets ground-robot collision avoidance and real-time safety monitoring.

[571] arXiv:2611.09644 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
Lucia Pezzetti, Nicolas Lanzetti, Antonio Terpin, Florian Dörfler, Giorgia Ramponi
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)

We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.

[572] arXiv:2611.09646 [pdf, other]
Title: Fast and Actionable Classification of HPC I/O Time Series
Maxime Gonthier, Luan Teylo, Francesco Antici (RIKEN CCS), Mihail Popov, Francieli Boito (LaBRI, UB)
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

Input/output (I/O) is a major bottleneck for highperformance computing (HPC) performance. One of the challenges is the contention between jobs when sharing the parallel file system. However, tackling this issue depends on knowing the temporal behavior of jobs. In this paper, we propose a clusteringbased approach to characterize jobs' temporal I/O behavior. We propose SAGE, a lightweight method that cuts I/O traces into short windows and learns an alphabet from them. The trace then becomes a sequence of symbols, which we call ''genome'', and we use clustering to separate them into classes. We evaluate SAGE and its two-stage variant SAGE-2 on 819,771 real traces from 2 HPC systems. We compare them against other techniques from the state of the art on three metrics, including one we propose. Compared to K-shape, the best baseline available, SAGE-2 lowers the median intra-cluster metrics by 9.1% on average, and achieves this in 2 minutes of clustering time versus 3.8 hours, a 109x speedup. More importantly, clusters created by SAGE and SAGE-2 carry enough information to act on: we evaluate the use of the cluster centroids for I/O scheduling, and show that our approach can decrease I/O stretch by up to 24% compared to the state of the art (round-robin placement).

[573] arXiv:2611.09649 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Parallel Algorithms for Higher-Order Temporal H-Index Computation
Lutz Oettershagen
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

Ranking vertices by importance is a fundamental task in network mining. The H-index provides such a ranking by asking how many neighbors are themselves well connected; its higher-order temporal variant recursively applies this idea over time-respecting neighborhoods in temporal networks. Scaling its computation is difficult because the existing streaming algorithm intertwines temporal processing with H-index order, incurring maximum-degree-dependent costs and exposing little parallelism. We show that the temporal dependencies can instead be resolved once: each edge's time-dependent lookup is mapped to a fixed successor position, turning every H-index order into a parallel gather followed by a segmented suffix-H computation. Based on this reformulation, we derive a linear-work suffix-H algorithm, a parallel multicore CPU implementation, degree-adaptive GPU kernels, and a multi-GPU scheme that exchanges only distinct remotely queried states. Experiments on synthetic and real-world temporal graphs show that the reformulation alone is substantially faster than the streaming algorithm, and that GPUs add order-round speedups exceeding an order of magnitude over our multicore implementation on synthetic inputs with up to one billion temporal edges. On a 636M-edge Reddit network, eight GPUs compute 128 orders in 3.6 s of round time, whereas the streaming algorithm does not finish within an hour even at order 8.

[574] arXiv:2611.09650 [pdf, html, other]
Title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs
Zaheed Ahmed, Philip Makedonski, Jens Grabowski
Comments: 18 pages, 7 figures
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Mutation testing for deep learning (DL) faces a cost-realism trade-off. The pre-training approach produces realistic but computationally expensive mutants, whereas existing post-training operators modify trained models efficiently but produce mutants that less closely resemble real faults. This study asks whether the trade-off is necessary: can the weight-space effect of a fault-informed pre-training mutation operator be predicted from a trained model, without retraining it? We answer this question with TensorMutation, which represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) to predict parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline and reused across unseen models so that TensorMutation can generate executable mutants without retraining. We construct a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, including 25 newly curated subjects. TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects, TensorMutation achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches. The improvement over the post-training tool DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), whereas the differences from the pre-training tool DeepCrime and the norm-matched random control are not significant. These results show that fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models.

[575] arXiv:2611.09651 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Concurrent Use of FP32 and FP64 Computing Units on GPUs and Mixed-Precision Placement in WENO Reconstruction
Jun Hatayama, Daichi Mukunoki, Yusuke Onishi, Atsushi Sekimoto, Toshinori Kouchi
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

Scientific computing often requires FP64 arithmetic, although FP64 performance is limited on NVIDIA GPUs. Double-float (DF) emulation, which represents a value using two FP32 values with about 48 bits of significand, outperforms native FP64 where FP64 units are limited. On the other hand, mixed-precision strategies offload to FP32 the operations that do not determine accuracy. In both approaches, the native FP64 units remain idle during FP32 instruction execution. We investigated whether this idle resource can be recovered on A100, GH200, GB200, and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q. A microbenchmark shows that co-resident FP32 and native-FP64 kernels exceed the throughput of the faster kernel alone on A100 but not on GH200 and GB200; on RTX 6000 Blackwell, they do so against FFMA but, against DF emulation, only when the issue density of the DF kernel is reduced. We then tested whether this gain carries over to computing the WENO-Z reconstruction with the nonlinear weights in FP32 and the candidate polynomials in native FP64 (W32P64). We observe substantial overlap on A100, whereas GH200, GB200, and RTX 6000 Blackwell show little overlap. Importantly, the fastest placement does not always preserve the design accuracy of WENO-Z: for a one-dimensional entropy wave problem, W32P64 fails to achieve the design order of accuracy for WENO7 and WENO9. In contrast, DF emulation of the entire reconstruction comes close to it on the grids tested for WENO5, WENO7, and WENO9 while delivering a $2.51-3.94 \times$ speedup over FP64 on RTX 6000 Blackwell. For WENO5 on the two-dimensional Euler vortex problem the W32P64 error at $n=256$ is $1.26 \times$ that of FP64 and 1/104 of that of the all-FP32 reconstruction.

[576] arXiv:2611.09652 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
Ritik K. Badiya, Siladittya Manna, Ashmit Sinha, M Yashwanth, Anirban Chakraborty
Comments: Accepted at WACV 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.

[577] arXiv:2611.09655 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Decoupled Mode Connectivity for Base-to-Novel Generalization in Vision-Language Models
Imad Eddine Marouf, Khalid Oublal, Enzo Tartaglione, Stéphane Lathuilière
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 46 pages (10 main + references, appendix and checklist), 15 figures. Project page: this https URL Code:this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Prompt learning adapts vision-language models such as CLIP by optimizing a short learnable prompt. The cross-entropy objective pulls this prompt toward
base-class specialization, whereas generalization to unseen classes benefits from staying close to CLIP's zero-shot feature space. Because both objectives
act on the same prompt, their gradients conflict at convergence, and in our experiments no single-prompt loss design clearly improves on the cosine
baseline. We propose Decoupled Mode Connectivity (DMC), which gives each objective its own prompt. Starting from a base-trained prompt, DMC trains a
specialization prompt and a generalization prompt, and merges their text features with a fixed coefficient at test time, at the inference cost of a single
prompt. A linear mode connectivity (LMC) corridor in text-feature space keeps the classification loss low for every classifier interpolated between the two
endpoints, and a Visual Anchor KL term preserves CLIP's zero-shot class-similarity distribution of each image during specialization. We further argue that
such regularizers should satisfy class-permutation invariance (CPI), and show via Fano's inequality, in an idealized model, that violating CPI
lower-bounds the drop in novel accuracy by a term proportional to the mutual information between the prompt and the base-class labels. Across 11 datasets,
DMC improves the average harmonic mean of base and novel accuracy over MergeTune for both CoOp and KgCoOp, and its interpolation curves pass beyond the
single-prompt operating point, shifting the base-novel frontier rather than trading along it. Code is available at this https URL.

[578] arXiv:2611.09656 [pdf, html, other]
Title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting
Mathieu Vannimmen
Comments: 14 pages, 3 figures
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$.
